production.title: DeepSeek + REA Cloned Claude Code for FREE (Full Build)

narration:
Last month, one single developer shook the walls of Adobe,
a company worth close to 100 billion dollars.
Photoshop, Premiere, all in just one week.
He used about 8 Claude agents running at once.
But today, no paid Claude.
We're doing the same thing with free open models you can run tonight.
We're not rebuilding Photoshop.
We're rebuilding Claude Code itself.
An award-winning 3D website studied by the same free AI rebuilt in
its own code and checked screenshot by screenshot against the real thing.
Somewhere in the middle, the free AI hits a wall.
I'll show you the one line that gets you straight past it.
By the end, our free version goes head-to-head with the real Claude.
Same task, same clock, one winner.
Every AI coding tool has 2 parts.
The body, the app you type into, and the brain,
the AI model doing the thinking.
Today, the body is OpenCode.
The brain is DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Free.
It will run out.
When it does, we swap in GLM 5.3 Flash and carry on.
The third piece is REA, reverse engineer anything.
229 tools for looking inside software.
Plug it into an AI and the AI becomes the detective.
It doesn't copy code.
It doesn't write code.
It reads and reports back with proof.
Understand the recipe.
Don't photocopy the cookbook.
Install OpenCode, choose Windows x64, not ARM 64, and choose DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Free.
Paste the setup prompt and run REA's health check until it passes.
Today, a desktop app.
For native programs, REA needs a decompiler called Ghidra.
The wrong version came first; the AI swapped in 12.1.4 and tested Notepad:
853 functions mapped.
Green, 229 tools ready.
Before the big one, a warm-up.
This is igloo.inc.
It won site of the year at the awards.
Can a free AI study it and rebuild it in its own code?
For websites, REA drives a real Chrome browser, reads the layout, the scripts,
everything the page downloads, and takes screenshots.
Error 429.
OpenRouter's free models give you 50 requests a day for your whole account,
and an AI agent burns through requests fast.
So, I added Nvidia as a second provider, picked GLM 5.3 Flash,
and typed one line: Carry on from where you stopped.
It picked up exactly where it left off.
At one point, the AI proudly said, All 58 assets downloaded.
I opened the folder: 3 files.
So I sent one line back: Check the folder.
Never say a file is saved unless a folder listing shows it.
Try again.
This time, 105 real files, 17.7 megabytes.
Read reverse.md and rebuild the site scene by scene in your own code.
Never load the site's own JavaScript.
Plain HTML and 3.js, checking each scene in the browser before moving on.
Then compare screenshots of the real site and our copy.
The Claude app is the window.
Claude Code is the engine inside that window.
We're going after both, the window and the engine.
So, we changed the name, changed the icon,
and this stays a private learning build, not for sale, not for release.
I called it Kiln.
The AI then writes its own code from scratch.
Not one line of Anthropic's code makes it in.
Instead of repeating the same rules in every prompt,
the AI writes them once into agents.md.
Then there are 3 files: agents.md, the rules; features.md, our own engine and window;
and spec.md, every feature, one test each, and a 3-part build plan.
Then spec.md lands: every feature in the AI's own words, one test for each,
and a plan in 3 parts.
The build prompt is: Read agents.md, spec.md, and our saved versions.
Build the next unfinished part of the plan one feature
at a time and test each one with the self-check.
The self-check drives the real Kiln window, types a message,
and checks the file really got written.
Kiln is not allowed to say anything works until that robot hand says pass.
29 out of 29 passed.
Then: Done.
Version 1.0.
77 out of 77 checks passing.
Then DeepSeek ran out and wouldn't reset for 13 hours.
I switched to that model and typed: Read our files and saved versions.
Check any unsaved changes and carry on where the work stopped.
Nothing lost because every finished feature was already saved into Git.
77 out of 77 sounds perfect, right?
It wasn't.
The model picker wouldn't scroll.
4 features were missing: /compact, helper agents, MCP servers, and hooks.
The self-check only tests what the AI decided to build,
not what it was supposed to build.
Done is a claim.
Check the receipt.
One prompt fixed everything: Make the model picker scroll and add a search box.
Then build what's missing: /compact, helper agents, MCP, hooks, and retry on rate limits,
running the full self-check after each work.
40 minutes later, the self-check went from 77 to 102.
Every old test still passing.
25 new tests added and passing.
Then I asked Kiln which model it was using.
It said it wasn't powered by any separate large language model, which wasn't true.
Now it knows its own brain.
Same task, same clock.
On the left, the real Claude app.
On the right, Kiln on a free model.
Same empty folders.
Build a simple todo app as one file called todo.html.
Add tasks, remove them, delete one, refresh, and see how many are left.
Which one would you keep?
Free isn't unlimited or private.
The free DeepSeek model ran out for 13 hours.
Nvidia logs what you send.
Never put passwords or client code through a free cloud model.
One free app, one free brain, and REA.
The free AI studied the Claude app and Claude Code, wrote its own blueprint,
and built Kiln.
0 lines of code typed by me.
If you want more workflows like this, follow the channel.

research.summary: The November 11, 2026 Outskill video presents a tutorial for rebuilding Claude Code-like functionality with OpenCode, free or limited-cost models, REA, and a custom tool called Kiln. The central workflow is supported by the video’s transcript mirror and official tool documentation. The Adobe comparison is broadly factual but overstated: one developer released seven early-alpha Adobe-style applications in roughly a week using parallel Claude agents, but the projects were not full Photoshop or Creative Cloud replacements. The claim that GLM 5.3 Flash is free is not supported by OpenCode’s current pricing table, which lists it at $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens. The claim that REA has 229 tools is supported for REA 6.8.0-era installations, though the count varies by version.

claims.claim: The Outskill video was published on November 11, 2026, runs approximately 26 minutes, and demonstrates rebuilding Claude Code-like functionality with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GLM 5.3 Flash, REA, OpenCode, and a custom tool named Kiln.
claims.source_title: DeepSeek + REA Cloned Claude Code for FREE (Full Build) — transcript mirror

claims.claim: The tutorial reports a Kiln self-check progressing from 77/77 initial tests to 102/102 after missing features were fixed. This is a claim made by the video and its transcript mirror, not an independently reproduced benchmark.
claims.source_title: DeepSeek + REA Cloned Claude Code for FREE (Full Build) — transcript mirror

claims.claim: REA is an MCP-based reverse-engineering toolkit that connects AI agents to tools for inspecting native binaries, JavaScript and Electron applications, .NET assemblies, and websites. Its documentation says analysis runs locally and returns evidence and limitations for conclusions.
claims.source_title: REA official GitHub repository

claims.claim: The claim that REA exposes 229 tools is accurate for the REA 6.8.0-era tool catalog. Official repository issue data records 229 advertised MCP tools, while later version 6.9.0 data records 255, so the number is version-dependent.
claims.source_title: REA GitHub issue: schema and tool-count comparison

claims.claim: REA does not itself automatically produce a finished software clone. Its official workflow is to inspect an application, return evidence, and let the connected coding agent implement a similar feature or behavior.
claims.source_title: REA official GitHub repository

claims.claim: OpenCode’s official model table lists DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Free as free for both input and output, but the documentation says the free availability is for a limited time.
claims.source_title: OpenCode console models documentation

claims.claim: The video’s description of GLM 5.3 Flash as free is not supported by OpenCode’s current official model table. That table lists GLM 5.3 Flash at $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens.
claims.source_title: OpenCode console models documentation

claims.claim: The Adobe story is based on ArtCraft, a project by developer Brandon Thomas. Reporting says seven Adobe-style applications were released under the ArtCraft brand between September 30 and October 1, 2026, including Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere Pro, Lightroom, Acrobat Pro, After Effects, and InDesign-style tools.
claims.source_title: Someone Rebuilt Adobe in Rust with AI Agents. Is It Usable?

claims.claim: The claim that approximately eight Claude agents worked in parallel is supported by reporting on the ArtCraft workflow, which describes about eight Claude Opus 5.5 agents working on independent subsystems while a human handled integration and testing.
claims.source_title: Someone Rebuilt Adobe in Rust with AI Agents. Is It Usable?

claims.claim: The Adobe apps were not complete replacements for Adobe Creative Cloud. The project’s reported self-assessment put professional daily-work parity at roughly 25% to 35%; 115 of 170 reference files reportedly rendered pixel-identically in one Photoshop-style test, or about 68%.
claims.source_title: Someone Rebuilt Adobe in Rust with AI Agents. Is It Usable?

claims.claim: The ArtCraft apps were described as early-alpha software with substantial bugs and missing features. Independent testing coverage warned that the projects should not yet be treated as reliable professional replacements for Adobe applications.
claims.source_title: I tried those free AI-coded Adobe Creative Cloud clones, and they have some big problems

claims.claim: Adobe’s market value was approximately in the high-$80-billion to roughly $90-billion range around November 23–24, 2026, so the video’s phrase 'close to a hundred billion dollars' is directionally reasonable but should not be presented as an exact current valuation without a timestamp.
claims.source_title: Adobe market-cap data

core_fact.fact: On November 11, 2026, Outskill published a tutorial showing how it used OpenCode, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, REA, and other model providers to study Claude Code’s visible behavior and build a separate Claude Code-like tool called Kiln, including a reported 102/102 self-check result after fixes.
